newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Mortgage corp to insulate HK from rate shocks - Yam.
newsitem.headline: Mortgage corp to insulate HK from rate shocks - Yam.

text.p: Hong Kong's proposed Mortgage Corporation could help insulate the economy from interest rate fluctuations as more homeowners take out fixed-rate loans, said Hong Kong Monetary Authority chief executive Joseph Yam.

"To the extent that (the Mortgage Corp) would in time result in a higher proportion of mortgages being on fixed interest rates, there will be a greater degree of insulation of mortgage payers from interest rate fluctuations," Yam told the Hong Kong Economic Association in an address Tuesday.

"And to the extent that fixed interest rate borrowings become more readily available and popular, there will also be a greater degree of insulation for the economy as a whole from interest rate fluctuations," he said.
This is because a mortgage corp should be well placed to tap long-term savings through the issue of fixed-rate debt.

Proceeds of the fixed-rate issues would in turn be used to acquire fixed rate mortgage loans, which will "hopefully be greater encouragement for banks to offer and market fixed rate mortgage loans to home buyers," said Yam.
Most Hong Kong banks currently prefer to offer customers mortgage loans with floating interest rates in order to lessen the banks' own interest rate risk.

"The fact that borrowing and lending in Hong Kong generally, and in the mortgage sector particularly, operate predominantly on floating rates of interest is, in my opionion, not entirely satisfactory from the point of view of monetary stability," said Yam.

Under a fixed-exchange rate regime, borrowers that have interest payments subject to short-term fluctuations can be hurt if short-term interest rates must be adjusted sharply to defend the currency, Yam pointed out.
Property related loans make up a large share of Hong Kong private and institutional borrowing, so the economy as a whole can be vulnerable to such interest rate fluctuations.
The home ownership ratio in Hong Kong has increased to 45 percent at present from just 27 percent in 1980 and the HKMA expects this proportion to increase.
The share of mortgage loans in the total domestic loan portfolio of the banking sector has increased from less than 10 percent to well over 15 percent in the past 15 years, Yam said.
If lending for property development and investment is included, property related-loans now account for about 40 percent of total domestic loans, he said.

The HKMA expects the Mortgage Corp to be formally established and its board of directors appointed in the first half of 1997. Market operations are expected to commence in the second half of next year.
